preamble: The voiced palatal plosive [ɟ] becomes the voiced postalveolar fricative [ʒ] through spirantization. The clearest case is Arabic jīm. It is reconstructed as palatal [ɟ] (or [ɡʲ]) by the Quranic period, and after the early conquests it yielded [ʒ] in urban Levantine and most Northwest African dialects, alongside [d͡ʒ], [ɡ] and retained [ɟ] elsewhere (Watson 2002). French jour (< diurnum) reaches [ʒ] through a different chain, [j] > Old French [d͡ʒ] > [ʒ] (c. 1250–1300), so it belongs under j_affricate_to_zh rather than here.

examples.note: جمل 'camel'; Watson (2002) reconstructs jīm as /ɡʲ/ or /ɟ/ by the time of the Quran, later yielding /ʒ/ in the Levant and Northwest Africa; Standard Arabic /d͡ʒamal/, Egyptian /ɡamal/.

sources: Watson, J. C. E. (2002). The Phonology and Morphology of Arabic. Oxford University Press. https://doi.org/10.1093/oso/9780199257591.001.0001
